value.overview: The Harpy Eagle is one of the largest and most powerful forest eagles in the world. It is a specialized predator of tropical forests, using its broad wings and extremely strong feet to hunt mainly in the canopy. The species has a distinctive double crest, bold black-and-white plumage, and a gray upper breast band. Harpy Eagles require extensive mature forest and reproduce slowly, making them especially vulnerable to habitat loss and persecution.
value.classification: The Harpy Eagle belongs to the eagle and hawk family Accipitridae and is the only living species in the genus Harpia. Its scientific name is Harpia harpyja.
value.identification: Adults are unmistakable large eagles with a broad wingspan, a pale gray head, a dark double crest, a black back, and a white underside crossed by a broad black chest band. The tail is long and barred. Their legs are thick and powerful, with exceptionally large talons adapted for grasping monkeys and sloths. Females are substantially larger than males. Immature birds are paler overall and gradually develop adult plumage over several years.
value.rangeHabitat: The Harpy Eagle formerly ranged from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America. It inhabits extensive, mature, humid lowland rainforest, especially areas with tall emergent trees suitable for nesting and a rich population of arboreal mammals. In Costa Rica, it historically occurred in wet lowlands and forested mountain slopes, including Caribbean and southern Pacific regions. It is now extraordinarily rare or possibly extirpated there; occasional reports and potentially suitable remnant habitat are associated with the Osa Peninsula, northern lowlands near Nicaragua, the Caribbean region, and remote Talamanca forests.
value.migrationStatus: The Harpy Eagle is generally resident and non-migratory. In Costa Rica it is not considered a regular migrant; any remaining individuals would be expected to occupy large forest territories year-round, although records are extremely scarce and the present national status is uncertain.
value.breeding: Harpy Eagles form long-term pair bonds and usually nest in very tall emergent trees. The nest is a large platform made of sticks and is often reused and enlarged over many years. The female generally lays one egg, and breeding is slow: pairs may raise only one young every two to three years. Young birds remain dependent on their parents for an extended period, so loss of an adult or nesting tree can have serious effects on population recovery.
value.dietFeeding: The species is a high-level canopy predator. Its diet consists mainly of medium-sized and large tree-dwelling mammals, especially sloths and monkeys, along with some other arboreal vertebrates. It hunts from concealed perches or moves through the canopy, using its broad wings for maneuvering among trees and its powerful talons to seize prey. A large, intact forest is needed to provide sufficient prey and suitable hunting areas.
value.behavior: Harpy Eagles are usually solitary or found in pairs and spend much of their time perched quietly in the upper canopy. They are powerful fliers but are not normally seen soaring for long periods like many open-country eagles. Adults defend very large territories, and their low population density makes encounters uncommon. Their deep forest lifestyle, slow reproduction, and dependence on mature trees make them difficult to monitor and particularly sensitive to disturbance.

conservation.populationTrend: Declining globally, with severe local losses and extirpations across much of Central America. The number of surviving Harpy Eagles in Costa Rica is unknown, and any remaining population is expected to be extremely small and isolated.
conservation.threats: The principal threats are destruction and fragmentation of mature rainforest, removal of large nesting trees, hunting and persecution, and depletion of arboreal prey. In Costa Rica, historical deforestation and hunting greatly reduced the species. Its slow breeding rate and very large territory make natural recovery difficult when populations become isolated.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and reconnect large areas of mature forest, especially in the Osa Peninsula, northern lowlands, Caribbean forests, and Talamanca region. Prevent hunting and disturbance near suspected nests, conserve large emergent nesting trees, and support systematic surveys using local communities, protected-area staff, and responsible reporting of sightings. Any future reintroduction effort should follow rigorous feasibility studies, habitat protection, prey assessment, and long-term monitoring.
